title: Hero's steam-driven rotating sphere and its uncertain purpose
period: Roman-period textual tradition, conventionally c. first century CE but exact authorial date uncertain; 1851/2023 reception used only to interpret the evidence
summary: The transmitted device specifies rotation. Productive deployment and economic comparisons are absent from the inspected passage.

stages.invention: Description preserved, but inventorship and original date not secured.
stages.feasibility: A physically intelligible described mechanism; no reconstruction or ancient performance test conducted in this contribution.
stages.deployment: No productive installation established by the inspected sources.
stages.diffusion: No adopter population or rate available.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Intellectual/display purpose is plausible; actual frequency of use unknown.
stages.displacement/reversal: No operating industry is established from which a reversal could be inferred.

mechanisms: Purpose determines the relevant performance criterion.
Moving from rotation to productive service requires additional evidence about loads, duration and buyers.
counterevidence: Other Heronian devices are practical; absence of one application in a transmitted text is weak evidence about all ancient uses.

episode.technology_configuration: Heated cauldron feeding a pivoted sphere with opposing bent outlets, as described in Pneumatica II.11.
episode.task: Visible rotation; intellectual, demonstrative or performative purpose contested.
episode.population: Authorial/readership tradition; historical builders and users are not identified.
episode.interval: Ancient textual episode only; subsequent editorial reception is a separate interpretive subepisode.
contemporary_alternatives: Other mechanical demonstrations for teaching/display; productive water or muscle power only if the task is instead grinding or pumping (analytical comparison, not a documented purchaser choice).
episode.adoption_measure: One transmitted technical description; no adoption denominator or prevalence window.
episode.observation_limits: No original apparatus, user log, or output series; later translation and images mediate the record.

actors.chooser: Unknown: no ancient commissioner or buyer identified.
actors.payer: Unknown: no budget or patron specified in this passage.
actors.operator_maintainer: Hypothetical builder/operator in instructions; actual person's status and pay unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Unknown; no workforce or neighbouring users described.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown: instructions show no observed choice or compulsion.

labour.tasks: Construction, heating and attending the described apparatus; no demonstrated displacement of grinding or pumping work.
labour.entry_barriers: Metalworking and assembly implied by the design; no measured training or asset costs.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Unknown ownership, patronage and control of gains.
labour.transition: No identified workers or cohorts transitioning between tasks.
labour.evidence_limit: A technical text cannot establish jobs created, labour saved, wages or welfare.

title: Barbegal's watermill complex: seasonal operation and staged cessation
period: Second–third centuries CE; terminal reconstruction concerns selected western mills' final roughly 8–9 years
summary: Material traces establish operating watermills and changes in equipment; market destination and final abandonment cause remain uncertain.

stages.invention: No first-invention claim; the case concerns an installation.
stages.feasibility: Operational deposits and architecture support repeated use.
stages.deployment: Sixteen wheel positions in two trains; selected surviving casts.
stages.diffusion: No regional denominator; Barbegal does not establish commonness.
stages.scaling: Substantial integrated capacity, without adopted output tonnage.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Seasonal operation inferred; possible ship-biscuit market not confirmed.
stages.displacement/reversal: Different western flumes ceased in stages while water continued; later reuse occurs.

mechanisms: Water infrastructure and machinery complement one another.
Repair preserves capacity; water availability alone is insufficient.
Demand and seasonal operating schedules may interact.
counterevidence: Shared carbonate archive limits independence of studies; discharge, markets, ownership and the eastern train's exact fate are incompletely known.

episode.technology_configuration: Two trains of eight aqueduct-powered wheels; terminal evidence specifically from three western flumes.
episode.task: Grinding grain; final consumer and possible biscuit manufacture uncertain.
episode.population: Operators and consumers of this installation, identities and number unknown.
episode.interval: Second–third centuries CE, with distinct terminal subepisodes per flume.
contemporary_alternatives: Hand, animal and smaller watermills as contemporaneous technological alternatives; no evidence the owner explicitly priced and rejected them.
episode.adoption_measure: Installation configuration plus sampled isotope/microstratigraphic sequences. No population of eligible mills or percentage adoption.
episode.observation_limits: Wood decayed; carbonate preserves selected parts and years. Wheel positions are not year-round output.

actors.payer: Financing and ownership unknown; substantial construction does not identify public or private payer.
actors.operator_maintainer: Milling and woodworking/repair workers implied by physical interventions; legal status and pay unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Potential grain suppliers, consumers and workers, but identities and distributions not recovered.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown for Barbegal workers; Roman slavery elsewhere cannot determine their status.

labour.tasks: Grinding energy supplied by water; grain handling, millstone care, woodworking and flume adjustment persisted. Net labour change unmeasured.
labour.entry_barriers: Access to an appropriate supply/fall, machinery and repair competence; entry cost not quantified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Ownership and allocation of saved effort or revenue unknown.
labour.transition: Years of component replacement are visible; worker biographies or displacement duration are not.
labour.distribution: No observed wages, consumption distribution or compensation for displaced millers.
labour.evidence_limit: Capacity cannot be translated into employment eliminated or general emancipation from labour.

title: Rome's aqueduct service and the 537 milling emergency
period: Subepisode A: c. 97–early second century CE maintenance administration; subepisode B: siege of 537 CE
summary: Administrative evidence makes maintenance, funding and allocation visible; a later siege narrative describes different outcomes for drinking, bathing and milling.

stages.feasibility: Established urban conduits and mills, not just technical descriptions.
stages.deployment: Frontinus describes Rome's services and workforce; Procopius describes mills dependent on an aqueduct.
stages.diffusion: No inference from Rome to every Roman city.
stages.scaling: Maintenance and distribution arrangements support a large service; exact consumption not reconstructed.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Animal-driven substitution reportedly restricted by fodder shortage in 537; wells remained useful.
stages.displacement/reversal: Siege interruption and reported boatmill replacement; not proof of permanent universal aqueduct loss.

mechanisms: Recurrent finance, workforce, access and repair schedules complement physical assets.
Emergency substitution depends on resources required by each alternative.
counterevidence: Frontinus is prescriptive and self-presentational; Procopius is a single later narrative. The two subepisodes cannot be treated as one continuous panel.

episode.technology_configuration: A: aqueduct maintenance/distribution at Rome. B: aqueduct-fed Janiculum mills and reported Tiber boatmills during siege.
episode.task: A: reliable water delivery and allocation. B: grinding during blockade, distinguished from drinking and bathing.
episode.population: A: officials, enslaved work gangs and entitled water users. B: siege population and military organisers; exact coverage unknown.
episode.interval: Two explicitly separate episodes, c. 100 and 537 CE.
contemporary_alternatives: Wells and river for drinking, attested by Procopius.
Animal milling was a known but fodder-constrained option in 537.
Tiber boatmills reportedly substituted during siege.
episode.adoption_measure: Textual staffing and procedural account; narrative emergency sequence. No quantified diffusion or service-coverage denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Reported rules differ from enforcement; staffing is not employment trend; narrative sufficiency is not throughput.

actors.chooser: A: water commissioner, emperor and other authorities in defined legal roles. B: Belisarius according to Procopius.
actors.payer: A: public treasury, imperial purse and some water-right revenue. B: funds and requisition arrangements not specified.
actors.operator_maintainer: A: public/imperial enslaved specialists and contractors. B: boatmill builders/operators not individually identified.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Enslaved workers; water users without decision authority; households dependent on distributions; siege residents.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Enslaved maintenance workers did not have ordinary free-labour choice; precise coercion and resistance not measured. Household alternatives varied; siege constrained choice.

labour.tasks: Inspection, cleaning, masonry, piping and administration; boatmill assembly and tending in 537. Enslaved labour explicitly present in A.
labour.entry_barriers: Specialised work roles and controlled access to assets; actual training pathways unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Public/imperial ownership and grants shape control; individual worker bargaining power unmeasured.
labour.transition: No linked worker cohorts across the two widely separated episodes.
labour.distribution: Access was differentiated legally; no quantified welfare or wage change by group.
labour.evidence_limit: Do not infer freedom, consent or secure livelihoods from useful infrastructure; no employment multiplier calculated.

title: Early southeast Arabian falaj with an Iranian textual contrast
region: Southeast Arabia, especially al-Madam and Al Ain (present UAE)
period: Arabian first millennium BCE; Iranian channels described for a late third-century BCE campaign; later revival mentioned only as a contrast
summary: Local galleries show adaptation and limits. A separate Iranian narrative reports a long benefit horizon, without establishing a shared origin or universal governance system.

stages.invention: Multiple-origin and diffusion hypotheses remain contested.
stages.feasibility: Groundwater interception plus suitable gradient differs from mere underground conveyance.
stages.deployment: Excavated Arabian installations associated with settlements; Iranian account is textual.
stages.diffusion: No universal direction or adoption denominator established.
stages.scaling: Regional settlement associations are not a quantified output expansion.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Conditions and source depths vary; wells remain a named alternative in the synthesis.
stages.displacement/reversal: Deepening and later silting/abandonment at al-Madam; later deep galleries are not assumed a direct continuous lineage.

mechanisms: Groundwater and gradient constrain feasible operation.
Durable benefit rights could encourage investment, but that causal reading is untested.
counterevidence: Poor dating and excavation in Iran can distort apparent priority; similar gallery forms fit diffusion plus adaptation as well as independent innovation.

episode.technology_configuration: A: early Arabian shafts-and-gallery water catchment, with al-Madam alteration sequence. B: northern Iranian underground channels in Polybius, water source not specified.
episode.task: Bring water to settlement/cultivation; in Polybius also water access on a military route.
episode.population: A: excavated settlements' users. B: people reported as beneficiaries of earlier Persian cultivation grants; no census.
episode.interval: Distinct regional episodes within the first millennium BCE.
contemporary_alternatives: Surface-water channels where an appropriate source exists; unavailable at some sites rather than demonstrably rejected.
episode.adoption_measure: Archaeological occurrence and local relative sequence, plus one narrative report. No number of eligible settlements or diffusion rate.
episode.observation_limits: Many galleries undated or repeatedly altered; collecting and conveying functions can be confused; written and excavated populations differ.

actors.chooser: Arabian builders and allocation authorities incompletely identified; Persian rulers reported as grantors in a separate literary story.
actors.payer: Arabian financing unknown; Polybius reports substantial expense by builders but gives no accounts.
actors.operator_maintainer: Diggers, cleaners and water users required; named people, remuneration and labour status unknown in these ancient episodes.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Dependent cultivators and downstream/competing users are plausible affected groups, not measured participants.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown: later communal water rules cannot be projected onto first-millennium BCE settlements.

labour.tasks: Excavation, depth adjustment, clearing and water distribution; reduced recurring lift at a suitable gravity outlet is a physical inference, not measured net labour saving.
labour.entry_barriers: Local water-location, gradient-setting and excavation knowledge; access rights and capital may matter but are not quantified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Polybius's cultivation right is reported; actual title, inheritance conditions and division of benefits unknown.
labour.transition: Physical adaptation sequence known through synthesis; no individual livelihood transitions.
labour.distribution: No ancient distribution of work, water, land or surplus by group established.
labour.evidence_limit: Do not infer egalitarian community organisation, free work or indefinite sustainability from a gravity-fed design.

title: Dujiangyan's late Han repair evidence and the limits of longevity claims
region: Min River and Chengdu Plain, Sichuan, China
period: Ancient focus: conventional third-century BCE foundation through late Han inscriptions of 168/199 CE; 2020 model is a separate analytical comparator
summary: Late Han evidence supports organised upkeep. Modern hydraulics clarifies physical processes but cannot close gaps in ancient institutional or configuration history.

stages.invention: Conventional Li Bing/Qin foundation is context, not a precise date newly established here.
stages.feasibility: Modern geometry offers a modelled mechanism; ancient functioning cannot be quantified from that model.
stages.deployment: Inscription-based maintenance attestations by late Han.
stages.diffusion: No count of Chinese irrigation adopters or direct transmission to other systems.
stages.non-adoption/niche: No matched alternative design choice observed.
stages.displacement/reversal: Continuity in naming and later use does not prove unchanged operation or no interruptions.

mechanisms: Flow and sediment depend on local geometry.
Repeated repair requires labour organisation and appropriate timing.
Official and ritual authority can coexist with technical work.
counterevidence: Qin maintenance continuity is inferred, rules have disputed dates, and the model needs further validation and does not reproduce every ancient configuration.

episode.technology_configuration: A: late Han repair episodes interpreted from inscriptions. B: 2020 numerical geometry of Fish Mouth, Feishayan, Baopingkou and associated channels.
episode.task: A: maintain water diversion. B: explain water/sediment partition under specified flows.
episode.population: A: local water officials and repair workforce; household population unknown. B: simulated hydraulic system, not ancient adopters.
episode.interval: A: 168/199 CE attestations with uncertain earlier continuity. B: modern model only.
contemporary_alternatives: Different diversion geometries or water sources are possible analytical alternatives; no contemporary rejected proposal established.
Dredging plus repair rather than permanent avoidance of maintenance.
episode.adoption_measure: Inscription readings mediated by Peng; numerical experiment. Neither gives a continuous adoption or uptime series.
episode.observation_limits: Modern simulation and later traditions cannot fill centuries of missing records; original inscription rubbings not checked.

actors.chooser: Water officials and appointed supervisors in Peng's late Han account; exact foundation decisions not reconstructed.
actors.payer: Ancient detailed funding unknown; Peng explicitly lacks pre-Tang treasury records. Later funding cannot be imputed to Han amounts.
actors.operator_maintainer: Organised repair workers with labour-obligation interpretation; names and categories selectively commemorated.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Cultivators, obligated households and other river users; no quantified allocation of benefits and burdens.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Corvée interpretation indicates constrained choice for some workers; no basis to treat all participation as voluntary or all work as unpaid.

labour.tasks: Dredging, embankment work, monitoring and coordination. Ancient episodes show labour mobilisation; modern model does not count historical work hours.
labour.entry_barriers: Specialist knowledge and official organisation; actual occupational recruitment unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Official supervision is attested in interpretation; worker bargaining and allocation of crops/water unknown.
labour.transition: No individual or cohort transition series; institutional evolution cannot substitute for one.
labour.distribution: No ancient wage, mortality, household burden or irrigated-benefit distribution measured.
labour.evidence_limit: Longevity cannot establish that maintenance work was light, fairly distributed or universally beneficial.

title: Dholavira's runoff storage and uneven urban service
region: Khadir Island, Kachchh, Gujarat, South Asia
period: Third to mid-second millennium BCE; ICOMOS phases include gaps and a final occupation around 1500–1450 BCE
summary: Excavated reservoirs demonstrate deployed water management, while new GPR identifications and damage causes remain hypotheses. Political organisation and service distributions are largely unrecovered.

stages.invention: No first reservoir or unique-inventor claim.
stages.feasibility: Large excavated storage and diversion structures are material evidence; water balances not reconstructed.
stages.deployment: Combined water features with construction phases.
stages.diffusion: One site; no denominator for Harappan adoption.
stages.scaling: Reservoir construction associated with an expansion phase; output/population capacity not estimated.
stages.non-adoption/niche: No demonstrated decision to reject perennial-supply technology; environment and alternatives differ.
stages.displacement/reversal: Unrestored damage and settlement gaps in ICOMOS's narrative; cause not identified.

mechanisms: Storage shifts water availability across time, conditional on inflow and retained capacity.
Changing settlement demand and maintenance can interact.
Feature identification and causal explanation require separate tests.
counterevidence: GPR offers multiple structural interpretations; decline narratives are not independently re-dated here. Other water sources could persist when monumental features cease.

episode.technology_configuration: Excavated runoff/rainwater storage, stream diversion and drains; separately, hypothesised buried water features east of the East Reservoir.
episode.task: Store and distribute episodic water while managing runoff.
episode.population: City residents and producers across changing occupation phases; total and group coverage unknown.
episode.interval: Phased third–mid-second millennium BCE system, not a single unchanged installation.
contemporary_alternatives: Wells are present in the site's water-management description.
Different storage/distribution arrangements are possible; no ancient procurement comparison survives in inspected sources.
episode.adoption_measure: Excavated structures and phased settlement narrative; GPR is a modern detection sample, not an adopter census.
episode.observation_limits: Structures do not determine ownership or use allocation; geophysics alone cannot date damage; source dates differ.

actors.chooser: Unknown: size and planning do not identify a ruler, council or neighbourhood decision mechanism.
actors.payer: Unknown: no construction or maintenance accounts inspected.
actors.operator_maintainer: Builders, cleaners and distributors inferred from function; identities, status and pay unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Residents and producers dependent on stored water; differential access not reconstructed.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown; cannot infer consent or hydraulic coercion solely from monumental remains.

labour.tasks: Excavation, stonework, runoff control, cleaning and distribution; proportions paid/unpaid and labour displaced unknown.
labour.entry_barriers: Stoneworking and construction competence evident indirectly; recruitment, exclusion and asset ownership not recoverable here.
labour.bargaining_ownership: No established ownership or bargaining arrangements.
labour.transition: Settlement phases show aggregate reorganisation, not individual occupational transitions.
labour.distribution: No per-household reliability, labour burden or livelihood distribution quantified.
labour.evidence_limit: No supported claim that city growth improved every resident's welfare or that water failure alone caused migration.
